The smell of turpentine and linseed oil usually calmed Liam, but tonight it only served as a sharp reminder of the betrayal he was committing. He stood in the dim light of his studio, a half-finished canvas of the family’s textile mill looming before him, its red bricks bleeding into the night sky. The door to the studio creaked open, not with the gentle knock of his mother, but with the heavy, authoritative thud of his father, Arthur. Arthur didn’t look at the painting; he looked at the ledger on the table, its pages filled with the red ink of declining profits that Liam’s absence had exacerbated. "The board meets in an hour, Liam," Arthur said, his voice devoid of warmth, carrying the weight of three generations of expectation. "You will be there. You will sit in the chair that bears your name, or you will leave this house and never come back." The ultimatum hung in the air, thick and suffocating. Liam’s hand tightened around his brush, the bristles snapping under the pressure. He looked at the canvas, then at his father’s cold, expectant eyes. The rift wasn't just a crack anymore; it was a chasm, and he was standing on the edge, holding a brush that felt heavier than any tool he had ever used. He had to choose: the legacy that was suffocating him, or the art that was killing his family’s business.

Regarding your priority question: Sugar tastes sweet. It provides a quick burst of energy and a pleasant, comforting sensation on the tongue, often described as pure and simple, though the intensity can vary from a delicate hint to an overwhelming cloying richness depending on the concentration and type of sugar.
